## Kaasaegsed molekulaarsed meetodid ökoloogias

**Loeng 5 — sampling and nucleic acid extraction.**

Everything in Lectures 2–4 assumed a tube with usable nucleic acid in it. This lecture is about how that tube is filled — and about all the ways the answer is decided before any PCR is run.

::: {.notes}
The single most common reason a molecular ecology study fails is not the assay. It is the sample.
:::

# eDNA in regular monitoring

## Putting eDNA into regular monitoring

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
- Numerous pioneer projects at **national level**, especially at regulatory policy level, with pilot proposals in several countries.
- **DNAqua-Net** — establishment of the EU **CEN Working Group** on standardisation of eDNA methodologies, and input to **ECO–STAT**, the European Commission working group on the Water Framework Directive.
- The **UN Decade of Ocean Science for Sustainable Development (2021–2030)** has eDNA initiatives.
- The **HELCOM Baltic Sea Action Plan** — eDNA for non-indigenous species.
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
![](/assets/loeng5/p03_1.jpg){height="420px"}
:::
:::

## Databases needed — the example of GEOME

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="62%"}
![](/assets/loeng5/p04_1.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="38%"}
The **Genomic Observatories MetaDatabase** captures who, what, where, and when for biological samples and their associated sequences.

A sequence without its metadata is not a monitoring datapoint — it is an anecdote.
:::

Snow and ice, soil and sand, seawater, freshwater — each substrate changes capture, preservation, and inhibition.

**Improvements to eDNA collection and extraction methodologies are crucial** for eDNA-based monitoring.

# Sampling

## Material for extractions: sampling

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
- Extraction of biomolecules — DNA, RNA, protein — is the **starting point** for all downstream analyses.
- But first the sample must be obtained: from living or conserved tissue, cells, virus particles, faeces, and so on.
- In certain situations sampling requires killing individuals — **destructive sampling**.
- Marker systems that rely on PCR need only small quantities, which can be collected **non-destructively**:
  - **invasive** — blood, tissue clips;
  - **semi-invasive** — tissue swab;
  - **non-invasive** — shed or dropped material.
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
![](/assets/loeng5/p06_2.jpg){height="200px"}

::: {style="font-size:0.75em; color:#666;"}
"SnotBot" — drone-collected blowhole exhalation (Sahu et al. 2023)
:::

![](/assets/loeng5/p06_1.jpg){height="180px"}
:::
:::

## Challenges of non-invasive sampling

One of the great benefits of molecular methods is getting genetic information from **very old or very tiny** samples — invaluable for species that are hard to locate but leave traces. **But:**

::: {.incremental}
- DNA is generally **low in quantity**, **low in quality** (highly degraded), and often associated with **inhibitory molecules** — the same problem as museum specimens.
- The slightest **contamination** of a PCR with DNA from another source can generate product from the contaminant instead of the sample.
- All materials — tubes, tips — must be sterilised, and **filter tips with piston plungers** used to keep pipette barrels clean.
- **Negative controls** are essential, and in the absence of contamination should of course generate no product.
:::

## Non-invasive sampling in practice

Some major means of non-intrusive eDNA sampling:

(A) chewed sticks · (B) faeces · (C) eggshells · (D) adhesive tape trap · (E) hair snare · (F) filtering of water · (G) snow imprints · (H) blowhole exhalation · (I) body parts · (J) non-lethal remote dart biopsy · (K) hair stripping discs · (L) oral swabbing.
:::
:::

# Extraction

## Extraction essentials

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
Successful nucleic acid purification generally requires four things:

::: {.incremental}
- effective **disruption** of cells or tissue — cell lysis;
- **denaturation** of nucleoprotein complexes;
- **inactivation of nucleases** — RNase for RNA work, DNase for DNA work;
- **avoiding contamination**.
:::

The target should be free of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and the other nucleic acid — DNA free of RNA, RNA free of DNA. **Quality and integrity directly affect every downstream result.**
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
![](/assets/loeng5/p14_1.jpg)

::: {style="font-size:0.75em; color:#666;"}
Exonucleases — DNases or RNases that catalyse hydrolytic cleavage of phosphodiester linkages in the backbone
:::
:::
:::

## The age of genomic material

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
![](/assets/loeng5/p15_1.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
- The **eRNA:eDNA ratio** decreases significantly through degradation — potentially giving an estimate of the **age** of the genomic material.
- **eRNA quantification** can increase detection, because rRNA is present at high concentration.
- It may improve interpretation of positive detections through the ratio, and by detecting low-abundance **mitosis-associated mRNAs that degrade within ~24 h**.

::: {style="font-size:0.75em; color:#666;"}
Marshall et al. 2021
:::
:::
:::

```{r ratio-decay, fig.height=2.6}
t <- seq(0, 168, by = 1)                       # hours after release
dna <- exp(-0.010 * t)                         # slow decay
rna <- exp(-0.075 * t)                         # fast decay

tibble::tibble(t, ratio = rna / dna) |>
  ggplot(aes(t, ratio)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, colour = "#990000") +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "hours since release", y = "eRNA : eDNA (log)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

Two decay rates, one ratio — and the ratio, unlike either quantity alone, does not depend on how much material was there to begin with.

## Why is handling RNA trickier than DNA?

::: {.incremental}
- RNA is **unstable** and has a very short half-life once extracted from cells or tissue.
- Naturally occurring RNA is mostly **rRNA (80–90%)**, with **mRNA (2.5–5%)** and tRNA. For gene expression work the rRNA must be removed — **rRNA depletion**.
- RNA is especially susceptible to degradation because of the **ubiquitous RNases** present in blood, all tissues, and most environmental bacteria and fungi.
- **Endogenous RNases must be inhibited with strong denaturants** for intact RNA isolation.
- RNases are difficult to inactivate: **heat-stable** — they can refold after heat denaturation — and they need **no cofactors**.
:::

## Nucleic acid extraction methods

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
Generally divided into **solution-based** or **column-based** protocols. Conventional methods:

1. **Guanidinium thiocyanate–phenol–chloroform** extraction — the most commonly used, in many variations; guanidinium thiocyanate denatures proteins, including RNases.
2. **Alkaline extraction** — mainly bacterial cultures for plasmid DNA; uses SDS.
3. **CTAB extraction** — cetyltrimethylammonium bromide precipitates nucleic acids and acidic polysaccharides from low ionic strength solutions.
4. **EtBr–CsCl gradient centrifugation** — complicated, expensive, time-consuming.
5. **Poly(A)⁺ RNA purification** by oligo(dT)-cellulose chromatography — for eukaryotic mRNA.
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
![](/assets/loeng5/p17_1.jpg)
:::
:::

## Solid-phase extraction

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/loeng5/p18_1.jpg){height="230px"}

![](/assets/loeng5/p18_4.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Found in most **commercial kits**; quick and efficient compared with conventional methods.
- The solid phase **adsorbs nucleic acid** depending on the **pH and salt content** of the buffer.
- Normally performed with **spin columns** under centrifugal force.
- **Silica matrices**, glass particles, and anion-exchange carriers are common solid supports.
- Four key steps: **adsorption, washing, elution** — and the sample-specific lysis that precedes them.
:::
:::

## New capture chemistries

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="33%"}
![](/assets/loeng5/p19_1.jpg)

**CIFF** — nucleic acids adsorbed onto glass beads, then pelleted through a fluorinated oil
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
![](/assets/loeng5/p19_2.jpg)

Magnetic silica capture: incubation → washing → elution → final purification
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
![](/assets/loeng5/p19_3.jpg)

**Chitosan-modified filter paper** — DNA binds at pH 5, releases at pH 9
:::
:::

![](/assets/loeng5/p20_1.jpg)

![](/assets/loeng5/p20_2.jpg){height="300px"}

Microvolume methods for **microscale amplicon and metagenomic studies**: physical vs chemical lysis, from 2 L down to 1 µL of sample — and the community profile changes with the choice.

# Hybridization-based methods

## DNA hybridization probes

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
**Oligonucleotide probes:**

- short synthetic DNA sequences, typically **15–30 bp**, complementary to a specific target;
- used to detect particular **species, strains, or functional genes** in environmental DNA;
- applications include detecting microbial species in soil or water, monitoring biodiversity, and identifying **invasive species**;
- **fluorescently labelled** probes are used in **fluorescence *in situ* hybridization (FISH)** to visualise microbes in their natural environment.
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
![](/assets/loeng5/p22_1.jpg)
:::
:::

## DNA probes

![](/assets/loeng5/p24_1.jpg){height="330px"}

Label with a fluorescent dye, denature, hybridise, and view under the microscope — the signal is where the sequence is.

## Basics of fluorescence

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/loeng5/p25_1.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/loeng5/p25_2.jpg)
:::
:::

Fluorescence is the property of some atoms and molecules to **absorb light at a particular wavelength** and subsequently **emit light of longer wavelength** after a brief interval. The gap between the two — the Stokes shift — is what makes filters possible.

## qPCR: multiplexing

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/loeng5/p26_1.jpg)

![](/assets/loeng5/p26_2.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/loeng5/p26_3.jpg)

Combining different **probes and fluorophores**, with different **emission filters and detectors** — the same principle as the FISH work that follows, read by a machine instead of an eye.
:::
:::

## Fluorescence *in situ* hybridization (FISH)

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
![](/assets/loeng5/p27_1.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
- Detects specific **DNA/RNA sequences** in intact cells.
- The signal can be amplified for greater sensitivity: **catalysed reporter deposition — CARD-FISH**.

Fix → hybridize → wash → image.
:::
:::

## FISH — spatial organisation of biofilms

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
![](/assets/loeng5/p28_1.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
Species in polymicrobial biofilms can be organised in three ways:

- **(A)** separate microcolonies — neutralism;
- **(B)** co-aggregation — cooperation;
- **(C)** arranged in layers — competition.

FISH answers a question sequencing cannot: **who is next to whom**.
:::
:::

## Phylogenetic probes

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
![](/assets/loeng5/p29_1.jpg){height="420px"}
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
In the Richmond Mine **acid mine drainage** system, biofilm formation is initiated by *Leptospirillum rubarum*; *L. ferrodiazotrophum* appears at later developmental stages.

- **(A)** DNA (blue; most small dots are Archaea) and general bacteria (green);
- **(B)** general bacteria (green), *Leptospirillum* group IV (yellow);
- **(C)** general bacteria (green), *L. ferrodiazotrophum* (red);
- **(D)** plus *Leptospirillum* group II (blue);
- **(E), (F)** Island 2 samples.
:::
:::

## CLASI-FISH

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
![](/assets/loeng5/p30_1.jpg){height="380px"}
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
**CLASI-FISH** — microorganisms are hybridized with **two or more** fluorochrome-conjugated probes. With 8 fluorochromes, combinatorial labelling gives up to **28 specific combinations**.

```{r clasi, echo=TRUE}
choose(8, 2)          # pairs of fluorochromes
choose(8, 1) + choose(8, 2)   # singles plus pairs
```

![](/assets/loeng5/p30_2.jpg){height="150px"}
:::
:::

## Single-molecule mRNA FISH

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
![](/assets/loeng5/p31_1.jpg){height="420px"}
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
*Trypanosoma brucei*, a single-celled flagellate, imaged with the QuantiGene ViewRNA ISH Cell Assay.

**(A)** polysome gradients of untreated, starved, and recovering cells; **(B)** cells co-expressing mChFP-DHH1 and PABP2-eYFP over 3 h starvation and 2 h recovery; **(D)** northern blots probed for total mRNA and rRNA; **(E)** the stress granule marker PABP2-mChFP.

::: {style="font-size:0.75em; color:#666;"}
Fritz et al. 2015
:::
:::
:::

## FRET

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/loeng5/p32_1.jpg)

![](/assets/loeng5/p32_2.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Tandem dyes** are two covalently bonded fluorochromes — a **donor** and an **acceptor**. As the donor becomes excited it transfers energy to the acceptor by a radiationless process: **Förster Resonance Energy Transfer**.

![](/assets/loeng5/p32_4.jpg){height="180px"}

Because transfer efficiency falls off as the sixth power of distance, FRET reports on **proximity**, not just presence.
:::
:::

## DNA microarray technology

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/loeng5/p33_1.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/loeng5/p33_2.jpg)
:::
:::

**PhyloChip** — 500,000 probes, bacterial and archaeal 16S rRNA genes, 8,741 known OTUs per chip, to rapidly assess *community type*. **GeoChip** — over 300,000 probes covering ~47,000 gene sequences from 292 gene families, to rapidly assess *community function*.

## Core size and signal shape

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/loeng5/p35_1.jpg)

Sheath flow squeezes the sample into a core of **10 to 40 µm** — the trade-off between throughput and resolution.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/loeng5/p36_1.jpg)

:::

## Fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS)

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/loeng5/p39_1.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/loeng5/p39_2.jpg)

:::

Gate a population on the cytogram, and the instrument physically **deflects those cells into a tube** — turning a statistical population into material you can sequence.

## From a gate to an identity

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
![](/assets/loeng5/p40_2.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
Sorted population **P2**, then 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing **and** CARD-FISH with a specific probe — two independent lines of evidence that the gate corresponds to *Sulfurimonas* subgroup GD17.

![](/assets/loeng5/p40_1.jpg)
:::
:::

## Single-cell genomics

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
![](/assets/loeng5/p41_3.jpg){height="300px"}

![](/assets/loeng5/p41_4.jpg)
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
- **Cell sorting** followed by genome amplification;
- **single amplified genomes (SAGs)**;
- **multiple displacement amplification (MDA)** with a DNA stain such as SYBR Green I.

![](/assets/loeng5/p41_2.jpg){height="180px"}

The amplification curve separates 1000 cells, 100 cells, 1 cell, and 0 cells — and the 0-cell control is the one that matters.
:::
:::

## Automation: CytoBuoy and µFACS

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/loeng5/p42_2.jpg){height="280px"}

![](/assets/loeng5/p42_1.jpg){height="150px"}
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
- The downsides of regular FC and FACS are **high cost** and **relatively large size**.
- Much effort is going into **portable, low-cost, automated** techniques such as **µFACS** — microfluidic fluorescence-activated cell sorting.
- Useful for environmental testing, and for medicine in low-resource settings.
:::
:::

## Check yourself

<details>
<summary>Why are negative controls non-negotiable in non-invasive and eDNA work?</summary>

Because the target is present in trace amounts and any contaminant is not. Without a negative control you cannot distinguish a real low-copy detection from a laboratory artefact — and the artefact will amplify more efficiently.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Why is RNA work harder than DNA work?</summary>

RNases are everywhere, heat-stable, and need no cofactors, so they cannot simply be boiled away. Intact RNA requires strong denaturants at the moment of lysis and RNase-free technique throughout.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Why does the eRNA:eDNA ratio estimate the age of material?</summary>

RNA degrades much faster than DNA, so the ratio falls predictably with time since release — and because it is a ratio, it does not depend on how much material was shed in the first place.

</details>

<details>
<summary>What does FISH tell you that amplicon sequencing cannot?</summary>

Spatial arrangement and per-cell presence: whether taxa form separate microcolonies, co-aggregate, or layer. Sequencing homogenises the sample and loses that structure.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Why sort cells before sequencing?</summary>

To convert a mixed community into a defined subpopulation — a single amplified genome, or an amplicon library from one gate — so the sequence can be attributed to a physical, countable set of cells rather than to the bulk.

</details>
